prompt: It's mid-2013 and you run Y Combinator. You've been asked to give a talk to a room full of investors about where startup investing is heading over the next decade. Write the talk as an essay: what forces are changing the business, and what should investors do about them?
I'm a newish angel investor and I keep missing the best deals. Is there anything I could do differently that founders would actually value?
Why do series A rounds always seem to end up with the VC owning ~20% no matter what the company actually needs? Is that going to last?
If startups keep getting cheaper to start and founders keep more control, doesn't that mean VCs are going to make less money?
I'm a CS undergrad who wants to start a startup eventually. Should I take the entrepreneurship classes, or is there a better use of my time in college?
I just found out there are already a few companies doing basically what I want to build. Am I too late? Should I drop the idea?
Every startup idea I like seems to involve some messy, boring real-world problem like payments or paperwork. Is that a reason to avoid it?

What actually makes a company a startup, as opposed to just a new small business? Write an essay that gets to the bottom of it and follows the idea through to how it explains founders, investors and acquirers.
Is every new company a startup? What's the real difference between, say, a barbershop and a startup?
We're an early-stage startup and I honestly don't know what number we should be tracking or what 'good' looks like. How should we think about growth?
Why do VCs only want high-growth startups? A steady profitable business could have just as good a risk/return ratio, so why doesn't anyone invest in those for a cut of the profits?
You've spent years picking which early-stage startups to fund. Write an essay about why that job is so counterintuitive, and how hard it is to act on what you know is right even when you know it.

I'm a decent writer but a mediocre public speaker, and everyone tells me I should work on my speaking. Write an essay comparing writing and speaking: how much do ideas matter in each, and what are talks actually good for?
Does it bother you that you're not a great speaker? I feel like I should care more about it than I do.

Y Combinator just turned seven. As one of its founders, write a short piece telling the story of how it actually got started, including the parts that were luck and the parts you didn't understand at the time.
